Derivation from PyTorch’s reduction semantics: let m_it mark valid positions, n_i=Σ_t m_it, N=Σ_i n_i, and q_it=m_it w_it/Σ_t(m_it w_it). To preserve the global-position objective at uniform weights, use L=Σ_i(n_i/N)Σ_t q_it(ℓ⁺_it+ℓ⁻_it). Simply averaging row-normalized losses changes the objective by giving short and long histories equal mass. Preserve separately reduced positive/negative terms, their masks, denominators, and original coefficients independently; mean(positive)+mean(negative) differs by a factor of two from averaging their concatenation when counts match. Handle empty rows explicitly. [PyTorch loss reductions](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.modules.loss.BCELoss.html)

At uniform weights, compare baseline and rewritten scalar losses and every parameter gradient using identical parameters, batches, negative samples, and dropout randomness, before clipping or optimizer updates. Test unequal history lengths, padding, and separate masks; require finite values and numerical closeness. Select valid inputs before undefined operations such as division by zero or log(0); multiplying invalid losses by zero or masking their outputs afterward can still produce NaN gradients. Ensure normalization denominators are safe before division. [PyTorch autograd masking guidance](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/autograd)

Coefficient normalization preserves coefficient mass, not gradient norm: ∇L=Σ a_it∇ℓ_it depends on gradient magnitudes and alignment. Temporal reweighting can change direction, cancellation, and clipping frequency. Adam additionally depends on coordinatewise first/second-moment history and epsilon; clipping depends on the aggregate gradient norm. Thus normalization limits coefficient-scale drift but does not guarantee unchanged optimization scale or parameter updates. [Adam](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.15/generated/torch.optim.Adam.html), [gradient clipping](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.15/generated/torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_.html)
